0.1 Random variable, sample space, probability

blocks.html:
• The ideaA random variable is a number whose value you only learn after an experiment.
  • Roll a die: before rolling you don't know the number, after rolling you do.
  • That number is a random variable, usually called X.
blocks.text: The idea A random variable is a number whose value you only learn after an experiment. Roll a die: before rolling you don't know the number, after rolling you do. That number is a random variable, usually called X.

blocks.html:
• Sample space: all the values X can take.

    For a die: {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.

  • Event: any set of outcomes you might ask about, such as "the roll is 5 or more" = {5, 6}.

    The collection of all events you can ask about is the event space.

    For a die it is every subset of {1,…,6}, called the power set (there are 2⁶ = 64 of them).

  • Probability: a number between 0 and 1 for each event.

    For a fair die each face has probability 1/6, so P(X≥5)=P(X∈{5,6})=61​+61​=31​.

  • Non-negative random variable: one that can never be below 0, such as a distance, a count or a waiting time.

blocks.html:
• The ideaSuppose the average pocket money in a class is ₹50 and nobody can have negative money.
  • Could half the class have ₹500 or more?
  • No: those students alone would push the average to at least ₹250.
  • Knowing only the average already limits how many people can have huge values.
  • That is Markov's inequality.

Why "concentration inequalities"?

blocks.html:
• Often we do not know the full distribution of a random variable.
  • Maybe it is too complicated to compute, or we just don't have it.
  • We might only know its mean, or its mean and variance.
  • Concentration inequalities still let us say something useful: they put an upper limit on the probability of a rare, extreme outcome.
  • Equivalently, they say values usually concentrate near the typical value.

Reading the formula

blocks.html:
• Left side: the chance of a big value (at least a).
  • Right side: needs only the average.

  • The bigger the threshold a, the smaller the bound.

    Big values are rarer.

  • The bound is only useful when a>E[X].

    Otherwise E[X]/a≥1, and every probability is already at most 1.

Why it is true: a short proof
  • Split the average into outcomes below a and outcomes at or above a.
  • Every outcome contributes something ≥ 0 because X ≥ 0, and those at or above a contribute at least a each:
E[X]≥x≥a∑​xP(X=x)≥x≥a∑​aP(X=x)=aP(X≥a).
  • Divide both sides by a and you get Markov.
  • This is exactly the pocket-money argument written in symbols.

Every outcome contributes something ≥ 0 because X ≥ 0, and those at or above a contribute at least a each: E [ X ] ≥ x ≥ a ∑ ​ x P ( X = x ) ≥ x ≥ a ∑ ​ a P ( X = x ) = a P ( X ≥ a ) . Divide both sides by a and you get Markov. This is exactly the pocket-money argument written in symbols.

Key points to remember
Check that X is non-negative and the threshold is positive.
Divide the mean by the threshold to get an upper bound.
The bound is not an exact probability; a result above 1 is uninformative.
Learning goal: Use mean and variance to bound deviations on both sides.
Conditions to check

Reading the formula

blocks.html:
• ∣X−E[X]∣ is how far the outcome lands from the average, on either side.

    That is why there is an absolute value.

  • kσ means "k standard deviations away".
  • The chance of being at least k standard deviations away is at most 1/k2: at most 25 % for k = 2, 11.1 % for k = 3 and 4 % for k = 5.

Learning goal: Understand how sample size controls the error of a bounded average.
Conditions to check

• The ideaToss a fair coin 10 times and you might easily get 7 heads (70 %).

  • Averages of many independent things stick to their expected value, and the chance of straying drops exponentially fast as you add more samples.

Learning goal: Combine failure probabilities and compare related events.

The idea

  • Related events: if A can happen only when B happens, then A cannot be more likely than B.

• "A ⇒ B" (A implies B): whenever A happens, B has happened too.

  • So every outcome in A is also in B, which makes B the bigger set (superset).

  • Therefore P(A)≤P(B).

    The converse fails: B can happen without A.

Learning goal: Understand what dimensionality reduction must preserve.
Conditions to check
Big-O describes growth and does not determine a numerical target dimension without an explicit constant.
The distortion factor applies to squared distances.
A worst-case dimension guarantee can exceed the original dimension, in which case it offers no reduction.

• The ideaYou have a million points, each described by 10,000 numbers.
  • All you care about is how far apart the points are, for example to find nearest neighbours.
  • JL says you can describe each point with far fewer numbers and still have every pairwise distance correct to within, say, 10 %.
  • The magic: how few numbers you need depends on how many points you have, not on how many numbers you started with.

sections.title: Linear maps and the limits of exact preservation

blocks.text: Learning goal: See why reducing dimension requires approximate preservation.

blocks.html:
• The ideaShine a torch on a stick and look at its shadow on the floor.

  • Tilt the stick so it points straight at the torch and its shadow becomes a dot: its length is lost completely.
  • Any squeeze from more dimensions to fewer must crush some direction like this.
  • So keeping every length exactly is impossible.
  • JL asks for less: keep lengths approximately, and only for your n points.

1. Big data is expensive; randomness can make algorithms cheaper (Lesson 1).
  2. Markov, Chebyshev and Hoeffding bound the chance that a random quantity is far from typical, using progressively more information (Lesson 2–Lesson 4).
